pages.title: Not every metal releases hydrogen equally

blocks.text: Some metals react vigorously with water while others need steam or acid. Others do not release hydrogen from ordinary non-oxidising acids. This reflects different tendencies to supply electrons, not merely different appearances.
In a hydrogen-displacement reaction, the metal is oxidised and hydrogen is reduced. Reaction conditions and surface effects also influence the observed rate.

pages.transition: Write a water reaction with the correct electron and atom account.

pages.title: Active metals displace hydrogen from water

blocks.text: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). Sodium changes 0 → +1, while the hydrogen forming H₂ changes +1 → 0. Oxygen stays −2. Calcium similarly gives Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂.
Not all hydrogen in the water becomes gas. Some remains in hydroxide with oxidation state +1. Track the atoms in their actual products.
These are reactive-metal examples for understanding, not instructions for an unsupervised experiment.

pages.transition: Less active metals may react under different conditions.

pages.title: Acid displacement and its limits

blocks.text: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ gives net Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂. Chloride is a spectator in this simple reaction. Copper and silver do not normally liberate H₂ from dilute non-oxidising HCl under ordinary conditions.
An oxidising acid can produce different products, so the phrase metal plus acid always gives hydrogen is unreliable. The acid identity and conditions must be stated.

pages.transition: Halogen displacement follows competition for electrons rather than hydrogen release.

pages.title: Halogens differ in oxidising power

blocks.text: The usual oxidising-strength order in this chapter is F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. A suitable stronger halogen can oxidise the halide ions of a weaker one.

Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Chlorine accepts two electrons and is reduced; two bromide ions each lose one electron and are oxidised. The reverse displacement is not favoured under the same ordinary conditions.

pages.transition: A second example confirms the agent roles.

pages.title: Use half-reactions for a displacement

blocks.text: For Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂, reduction is Br₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Br⁻ and oxidation is 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻. Adding cancels two electrons. Br₂ is the oxidising agent and I⁻ is the reducing agent. Total charge is −2 on both sides.
I₂ is not the oxidant here merely because iodine is a halogen. Name the agents from the actual reaction direction.

pages.transition: Fluorine is unusually reactive toward water itself.

pages.title: Fluorine is an aqueous exception

blocks.text: Fluorine can oxidise water: 2F₂ + 2H₂O → 4HF + O₂. Fluorine changes 0 → −1, while oxygen changes −2 → 0. Therefore a simple aqueous halide-displacement comparison with F₂ is complicated by its solvent reaction.

Fluoride cannot be chemically oxidised to F₂ by the ordinary weaker halogens. Producing elemental fluorine requires suitable specialised conditions such as electrolysis, rather than a routine aqueous displacement.

pages.transition: Now consider one reactant serving as both oxidant and reductant.

pages.title: Chlorine can disproportionate in alkali

blocks.text: In cold dilute alkali: Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O. Chlorine begins at 0. It becomes −1 in chloride and +1 in hypochlorite, so one chlorine is reduced while the other is oxidised.

Charge balance is −2 on each side; oxygen and hydrogen also balance. Hypochlorite’s oxidising behaviour connects the reaction with bleaching chemistry, without requiring chlorine to be oxygenated before it can act as an oxidant.

pages.transition: Peroxide provides another clear oxidation-state split.

pages.title: Hydrogen peroxide shows both oxygen directions

blocks.text: In 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, all four O atoms start at −1. Two O atoms become −2 in water, gaining two bookkeeping electrons in total. Two O atoms become 0 in O₂, losing two in total. The electron changes balance.
The same original species supplies oxygen for both directions. This is different from a reaction where unrelated reactants supply separate oxidising and reducing elements.

pages.transition: The available oxidation states determine whether disproportionation is possible.

pages.title: Intermediate oxidation states allow two directions

blocks.text: An element in an intermediate state may be able to form both higher and lower states. Chlorine in suitable oxoanions can do this, but chlorine at its usual maximum +7 cannot be oxidised further in ordinary chapter chemistry.

An intermediate state is a possibility test, not proof that disproportionation occurs under all conditions. Thermodynamic stability and reaction conditions still matter. Fluorine cannot show a positive oxidation state in its ordinary compounds.
The initial state of elemental F₂ is zero, but that alone does not make its chemistry analogous to chlorine disproportionation; accessible product states must also be considered.

pages.transition: Revise displacement and disproportionation through their electron changes.

pages.title: Revision: compare the actual chemical roles

blocks.text: Metals can reduce hydrogen-containing species under suitable conditions. Halogens can oxidise weaker halide ions, with fluorine reacting strongly with water. The oxidant is reduced and the reductant is oxidised.

Disproportionation sends one element from one initial state to both a higher and a lower state. Verify balanced atoms, charge and total state changes; an intermediate state alone does not guarantee the reaction.

questions.question: In Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂, which species is reduced?
questions.answer: H⁺ is reduced from +1 to 0 in H₂.

questions.question: Why does copper not release hydrogen from ordinary dilute HCl?
questions.answer: Its reducing tendency is insufficient to displace hydrogen under those non-oxidising-acid conditions.

questions.question: Which is the oxidant in Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂?
questions.answer: Cl₂, because it gains electrons to form chloride.

questions.question: Why is aqueous F₂ not a simple halide-displacement reagent?
questions.answer: It oxidises water itself, complicating the desired displacement chemistry.

questions.question: Find chlorine states in Cl⁻ and ClO⁻.
questions.answer: Chloride is −1. In ClO⁻, x − 2 = −1 gives Cl = +1.

questions.question: Why is an intermediate oxidation state not enough to prove disproportionation?
questions.answer: Both directions must be chemically accessible and favourable under the conditions; oxidation-state bookkeeping alone does not establish reaction feasibility.
